patient.history_present_illness:
Mrs. L is a 61-year-old woman with post-polio syndrome who has experienced worsening weakness over 8 months that both she and her neurologist are concerned may represent ALS superimposed on her known post-polio syndrome.

She had paralytic polio at age 8 which primarily affected her left leg. She recovered partially with residual left leg weakness and atrophy. At age 53, she developed post-polio syndrome — new fatigue, slowly progressive weakness in her left leg and mild new bilateral arm fatigue, and widespread muscle fasciculations. This was confirmed by EMG showing chronic polio changes (enlarged motor units) with new active changes, and she has been managed with energy conservation and supportive care.

Over the past 8 months, however, the rate of progression has accelerated and new symptoms have emerged that are not consistent with typical post-polio syndrome (PPS): bilateral arm weakness with hand atrophy (PPS typically follows original polio distribution — her left leg), new RIGHT leg weakness not present before, tongue atrophy and fasciculations (never affected in her original polio), and new UMN signs (bilateral Hoffman signs, right Babinski) which CANNOT occur in PPS (a pure LMN process).

Her post-polio neurologist is highly concerned about superimposed ALS and has urgently referred for comprehensive evaluation.

results.title: Post-polio syndrome vs ALS: key distinctions
results.finding: Post-polio syndrome: LMN only, no UMN signs (Babinski/Hoffman impossible), restricted to originally-affected body regions, very slow progression. ALS: UMN+LMN combined, spreads beyond original distribution, progressive. New denervation in body regions not affected by polio is the EMG key for ALS diagnosis.

results.title: Incidence of ALS in post-polio patients
results.finding: ALS incidence may be mildly increased in polio survivors (possibly related to motor neuron vulnerability). When clinical features suggest ALS beyond PPS, EMG in non-polio-affected regions is diagnostic.

output.summary: UMN signs (Babinski, Hoffman) cannot occur in post-polio syndrome. New EMG denervation in body regions NOT involved in original polio establishes ALS diagnosis. PPS remains a concurrent but secondary condition.

contraindicated_actions: Attributing UMN signs to post-polio syndrome — PPS is a purely LMN process; UMN signs cannot occur
Delaying EMG in non-polio-affected regions — this is the diagnostic key
key_reasoning_points: Post-polio syndrome is a PURELY LOWER MOTOR NEURON late effect. It NEVER causes UMN signs. Any Babinski or Hoffman sign in a PPS patient requires a second diagnosis.

EMG interpretation strategy in PPS: identify denervation in body regions NOT affected by original polio. Chronic giant MUPs in old polio regions are expected; new active denervation in previously unaffected regions is ALS.
New corticospinal tract changes on MRI in a PPS patient (not present on prior study) strongly support superimposed ALS rather than PPS progression
